title: Two Orbits
statement:
Let $O$ be a point in the plane. Point $A$ moves at constant speed around the circle with centre $O$ and radius $16$ metres, completing one revolution every $20$ seconds. Point $B$ moves at constant speed around the circle with centre $O$ and radius $39$ metres, completing one revolution every $30$ seconds, in the same rotational sense as $A$.

Let $D$ be the closed disc with centre $O$ and radius $r$ metres, where $0 < r < 16$. As the points move, the segment $AB$ sometimes has at least one point in common with $D$. Each maximal continuous time interval during which this holds lasts exactly $20$ seconds.

The value of $r$ can be written as $\frac{a\sqrt{b}}{c}$, where $a$, $b$ and $c$ are positive integers, $a$ and $c$ are coprime, and $b$ is not divisible by the square of any prime. Find $a + b + c$.
hints: Whether the segment $AB$ meets the disc depends only on the size of angle $AOB$, not on the actual positions of $A$ and $B$. Think about how this angle changes over time.

Use relative angular speed. $A$ turns at $18^\circ$ per second and $B$ at $12^\circ$ per second, so the directed angle from $B$ to $A$ grows at a steady $6^\circ$ per second, and a $20$-second interval sweeps out $120^\circ$.

Contact is centred on the moment when $O$ lies between $A$ and $B$, where angle $AOB$ is $180^\circ$. So contact starts and ends when angle $AOB$ is $120^\circ$ and $AB$ is tangent to the disc. Then $r$ is the altitude from $O$ in the triangle with sides $16$ and $39$ enclosing $120^\circ$, which you can find using the cosine rule and the area.
solution: Let $\theta \in [0^\circ, 180^\circ]$ be the size of angle $AOB$, and let $d(\theta)$ be the distance from $O$ to the segment $AB$. The segment meets $D$ exactly when $d(\theta) \le r$. We first find how $d$ depends on $\theta$. By the cosine rule, $AB^2 = 1777 - 1248\cos\theta$, which is positive because the radii differ. For $0^\circ < \theta < 180^\circ$, since $OA < OB$, side $OA$ is not the longest side of triangle $OAB$, so the angle at $B$ is acute. The angle at $A$ fails to be acute exactly when $OA^2 + AB^2 \le OB^2$, which simplifies to $\cos\theta \ge \frac{16}{39}$. If $\cos\theta \ge \frac{16}{39}$, which includes the collinear case $\theta = 0^\circ$, the nearest point of the segment to $O$ is $A$. So $d = 16 > r$ and there is no contact. If $\cos\theta < \frac{16}{39}$, the foot of the perpendicular from $O$ lies on the segment, so $d$ is the altitude from $O$. This also holds at $\theta = 180^\circ$, where $O$ lies on the segment and $d = 0$. Computing the area in two ways gives $AB \cdot d = 624\sin\theta$, so $$d^2 = \dfrac{624^2 (1 - u^2)}{1777 - 1248u}, \qquad u = \cos\theta.$$ Differentiating $g(u) = \frac{1 - u^2}{1777 - 1248u}$, the numerator of $g'(u)$ is $$1248u^2 - 3554u + 1248 = 2(16u - 39)(39u - 16).$$ This is positive for $u < \frac{16}{39}$, since both factors are negative. So $g$ increases with $u$, and as $u$ decreases with $\theta$, $d$ is strictly decreasing in $\theta$ on this range. It runs continuously from $16$ at $\cos\theta = \frac{16}{39}$ down to $0$ at $\theta = 180^\circ$. Hence, for each $r$ with $0 < r < 16$, there is a unique angle $\theta_0$ with $\cos\theta_0 < \frac{16}{39}$ and $d(\theta_0) = r$. The segment meets $D$ exactly when $\theta \ge \theta_0$. Now $A$ turns at $18^\circ$ per second and $B$ at $12^\circ$ per second in the same sense, so the directed angle $\varphi$ from $B$ to $A$ increases at a constant $6^\circ$ per second. Contact holds exactly while $\varphi$ runs through $[\theta_0, 360^\circ - \theta_0]$ modulo $360^\circ$. This is one interval per $60$-second cycle, of length $\frac{360^\circ - 2\theta_0}{6^\circ}$ seconds. Setting this equal to $20$ gives $\theta_0 = 120^\circ$, and $\cos 120^\circ = -\frac{1}{2} < \frac{16}{39}$, as required. At $\theta = 120^\circ$ the cosine rule gives $AB^2 = 256 + 1521 + 624 = 2401$, so $AB = 49$. Then $r$ is the altitude from $O$, and comparing areas gives $$r = \dfrac{16 \cdot 39 \cdot \sin 120^\circ}{49} = \dfrac{312\sqrt{3}}{49}.$$ This is about $11.03$, so $0 < r < 16$ holds. Here $a = 312$, $b = 3$ and $c = 49$. Since $312 = 2^3 \cdot 3 \cdot 13$ is coprime to $49$ and $3$ is squarefree, the form is as required. The answer is $a + b + c = 364$. Why this works. clock-angles, monotonicity-analysis, law-of-cosines, sine-area-formula: the relative angle changes uniformly and the distance to the segment is monotonic in it, so the duration fixes the triangle at the moment of tangency, whose altitude is the radius.

solution_figures.alt: Two concentric circles with centre O and radii 16 and 39, the outer one shown as an arc, with A on the inner circle and B on the outer. At the moment contact begins, angle AOB is 120 degrees and AB = 49. Segment AB just touches the disc of radius r around O, at the foot F of the perpendicular from O, with a right angle at F.
